Assume the Axiom of Choice as in
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. Fix a finite
horizon $T>0$, a probability space with an increasing filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]], and an adapted
càdlàg (right-continuous with left limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued
process $N$ with $N_0=0$, $N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and jumps
$\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ outside one null event. Such a process is **simple**:
its event times are strictly ordered,
$0<T_1<\cdots<T_{N_T}\le T$. It is **locally finite** when it has finitely
many events on every finite interval.

For conditional-law calculations, the model supplies a measurable history
space $(\mathsf H,\mathcal G)$, an adapted measurable history random element
$H_t$ recording the initial information and events observed through time $t$,
and a measurable update map $h\mapsto h\oplus u$ that appends an event at
time $u$. Write $\mathcal H_t:=\sigma(H_t)$ and let $H_{t-}$ record only
events strictly before $t$. Relevant exogenous covariates are included in
the supplied history. Measurability has the meaning of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Predictability is
measurability for the predictable sigma-algebra generated by
$(s,u]\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$ and the time-zero generators, as in
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]].

The model supplies a probability kernel $K_{t,h}$ on $(t,\infty]$ for the
next event time given history $h$ at time $t$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]],
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]); its finite-time density
versions are jointly measurable in $(t,h,u)$. The value $+\infty$ means that
no later event occurs. If the finite-time measure is absolutely continuous
with respect to Lebesgue measure
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]],
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), let $f_{t,h}$ be its supplied
nonnegative Radon--Nikodym density
([[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]). Write
$S_{t,h}(u):=K_{t,h}((u,\infty])$ for its survivor and define its
**no-event conditional hazard** by
$$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u):=\frac{f_{t,h}(u)}{S_{t,h}(u)}\qquad\text{where }S_{t,h}(u)>0.$$
Assume these hazards are locally integrable on every finite interval. The
model also supplies a nonnegative predictable effective-intensity process
$\lambda^*$ compatible with these waiting-time hazards: for each history
$h$ at time $t$, on its supplied measurable no-event continuation up to
$u>t$, the pre-event intensity $\lambda^*(u\mid h_{u-})$ agrees with
$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u)$ for Lebesgue-almost every $u$. The jointly measurable
hazard representatives used in the event-density factors are these same
versions on their proper domains $u>t$. Compatibility with the predictable
process is a model requirement, not an evaluation of a waiting-time density
at its excluded left endpoint. This pre-event convention means the event
at $u$ does not change its own intensity.

The **temporal conditional-intensity model** requires both this
hazard-compatible conditional law and the separate counting-process
compensator contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]: if an at-risk
indicator $Y$ and intensity density $\lambda$ are separately specified, the
effective intensity is $\lambda^*=Y\lambda$; without an at-risk indicator,
it is $\lambda^*$. Then $A_t=\int_0^t\lambda^*(u)\,du$ is finite pathwise,
continuous, adapted and predictable, $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$, and $N-A$ is
a square-integrable martingale in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. At-risk exposure, if
present, is part of the effective intensity. The compensator clause is a
model assumption: a displayed hazard formula alone proves neither that a
process with this law exists nor that the martingale contract holds. No
stationarity or non-explosion claim follows from writing an intensity
specification.

Fix $n \ge 1$ and let $\lambda_n^*$ be the Lebesgue outer set function on $\mathbb{R}^n$
([[def-lebesgue-outer-measure]]). A set $E \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is
**Lebesgue measurable** when

$$\lambda_n^*(A) \;=\; \lambda_n^*(A \cap E) \;+\; \lambda_n^*(A \setminus E) \qquad \text{for every } A \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n .$$

This formula makes sense before any outer-measure theorem is invoked. Under
countable choice, [[thm-lebesgue-outer-measure-is-an-outer-measure-agreeing-with-volume]]
makes $\lambda_n^*$ an outer measure, and the displayed condition is then exactly
Carathéodory measurability in the sense of [[def-caratheodory-measurable-set]].

The family of Lebesgue measurable sets is written $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$,
and **Lebesgue measure** is the restriction

$$\lambda_n \;:=\; \lambda_n^*\!\restriction_{\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)} .$$

On the real line the subscript is dropped and $\lambda := \lambda_1$.

The quantifier over every test set $A$ is part of the condition, and no
hypothesis on $E$ is imposed before it is tested. That
$\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra and that $\lambda_n$ is a complete
measure on it are not part of this definition: they are proved, under the Axiom
of Countable Choice, in [[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]], which is
recorded in this item's `justified_by` because it is a statement about the
objects introduced here. Until that theorem the symbols $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$
and $\lambda_n$ name a family of sets and a restricted set function, nothing more.
For $f\in L^1[a,b]$, the function $I_f(x)=\int_a^x f$ is absolutely continuous.

Assume the Axiom of Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]).

Let $a<b$ and let $f\in L^1([a,b])$. Define
$$F(x):=\int_a^x f(t)\,dt\qquad(a\le x\le b).$$
Then $F$ is differentiable for almost every $x\in(a,b)$ and
$$F'(x)=f(x)$$
at every such point.

Let $A, B \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ with
$g[A] \subseteq B$ and let $f : B \to \mathbb{R}$, so that the composite
$f \circ g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ is defined. Let $c \in A$ be a limit point of
$A$ ([[def-limit-point-r]]) at which $g$ is differentiable
([[def-derivative]]), put $b := g(c)$, and suppose $b$ is a limit point of $B$
at which $f$ is differentiable. Then $f \circ g$ is differentiable at $c$ and

$$(f \circ g)'(c) \;=\; f'\bigl(g(c)\bigr)\,g'(c) .$$

**Both limit-point hypotheses are needed, and neither is automatic.** That $c$
is a limit point of $A$ is what makes $g'(c)$ and $(f \circ g)'(c)$ defined
symbols; that $b = g(c)$ is a limit point of $B$ is what makes $f'(b)$ one.
Nothing forces the second: $g$ may be differentiable at $c$ and send $c$ to an
isolated point of $B$, and there $f'(b)$ is not defined and the formula asserts
nothing.

**No case analysis appears anywhere.** The naive difference-quotient proof
writes $\frac{f(g(x)) - f(g(c))}{g(x) - g(c)} \cdot \frac{g(x) - g(c)}{x - c}$
and then has to say what happens where $g(x) = g(c)$, which may occur at points
arbitrarily close to $c$. Carathéodory's factorisation never divides by the
inner increment, so the difficulty does not arise.

Let $A \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, let $c \in A$ be a limit point of $A$
([[def-limit-point-r]]), let $f, g : A \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable at $c$
([[def-derivative]]) and let $\alpha \in \mathbb{R}$. Then:

1. $f + g$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(f+g)'(c) = f'(c) + g'(c)$;
2. $\alpha f$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(\alpha f)'(c) = \alpha f'(c)$;
3. $fg$ is differentiable at $c$ and $(fg)'(c) = f'(c)g(c) + f(c)g'(c)$;
4. if $g(c) \ne 0$ then, writing $A_0 := \{\, x \in A : g(x) \ne 0 \,\}$, the
   point $c$ lies in $A_0$ and is a limit point of $A_0$, the quotient
   $(f/g)|_{A_0} : A_0 \to \mathbb{R}$, $x \mapsto f(x)/g(x)$, is differentiable
   at $c$ as a function on $A_0$, and
   $$\bigl((f/g)|_{A_0}\bigr)'(c) \;=\; \frac{f'(c)\,g(c) - f(c)\,g'(c)}{g(c)^{2}} .$$

Each claim asserts two things: that the derivative on the left exists, and that
it has the stated value. Both are proved.

**Why claim 4 is stated on $A_0$.** The function $f/g$ is not defined where $g$
vanishes, and $g$ may vanish at points of $A$ far from $c$; restricting to $A_0$
is forced. That the restriction still has $c$ as a limit point, so that a
derivative there means anything at all, is not free either, and it is the last
claim of [[lem-sign-preservation-near-a-limit]] applied to $g$. The hypothesis
is $g(c) \ne 0$, not "$g$ vanishes nowhere".

**Everything is proved through
[[thm-caratheodory-characterisation]].** No difference quotient is estimated and
no limit theorem beyond continuity is used, so no choice principle is spent.
The four identities are four algebraic rearrangements of an increment, each
followed by a reading of [[thm-algebra-of-continuous-functions]].

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.
If $F,G\in AC[a,b]$, then $FG\in AC[a,b]$.

Assume the Axiom of Dependent Choice. If $F:[a,b]\to\mathbb R$ is absolutely continuous and $F'(x)=0$ for almost
every $x\in(a,b)$, then $F$ is constant.

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $(E_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}$ be a decreasing sequence of measurable sets for a measure $\mu$. If $\mu(E_{n_0})<+\infty$ for some $n_0$, then

$$\mu\left(\bigcap_{n\in\mathbb N}E_n\right)=\inf_{n\in\mathbb N}\mu(E_n).$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: Since $K_h((t,\infty])=1$, [F1] gives $S_h(u)=1-\int_t^u f_h(s)\,ds$. By [F2], $S_h$ and $\Lambda_h$ are absolutely continuous and $S_h'=-f_h=-\lambda_h^*S_h$ almost everywhere where $S_h>0$, while $\Lambda_h'=\lambda_h^*$ almost everywhere.

Fix a compact interval on which $S_h>0$. The cumulative hazard is bounded there, say $0\le\Lambda_h\le M$. By [F5], there is $L>0$ such that $|\exp(x)-\exp(y)|\le L|x-y|$ for $x,y\in[0,M]$. Since $\Lambda_h$ is absolutely continuous by step 1.1, for every $\varepsilon>0$ its absolute-continuity condition supplies $\delta>0$ such that every permitted finite family of subintervals with total length below $\delta$ satisfies $\sum_j|\Lambda_h(v_j)-\Lambda_h(u_j)|<\varepsilon/L$. Therefore $$\sum_j|\exp(\Lambda_h(v_j))-\exp(\Lambda_h(u_j))|\le L\sum_j|\Lambda_h(v_j)-\Lambda_h(u_j)|<\varepsilon,$$ so $G_h:=\exp(\Lambda_h)$ is absolutely continuous. By [F3], $G_hS_h$ is absolutely continuous and $(G_hS_h)'=G_h(\lambda_h^*S_h+S_h')=0$ almost everywhere. By [F4], $G_hS_h$ is constant. Its value at $t$ is $1$, so $S_h(u)=\exp(-\Lambda_h(u))$ wherever $S_h$ is positive.

Fix finite $U>t$ and suppose $S_h$ first reaches zero at some $\tau\le U$. On $[t,\tau)$, step 2.1 gives $S_h(u)=e^{-\Lambda_h(u)}\ge e^{-\Lambda_h(U)}>0$. Continuity of $S_h$ then gives $S_h(\tau)>0$, a contradiction. Thus the formula holds on all of $[t,U]$; substituting it into [F1] gives the density formula almost everywhere. Also $S_h(u)=K_h((u,\infty])$ decreases to $K_h(\{\infty\})$ along integer $u\to\infty$ by [F6]. Taking the limit in the survivor formula gives the two stated terminal-mass cases.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then

$$\mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^n) \;\subseteq\; \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n) :$$

every Borel subset of $\mathbb{R}^n$ ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]) is Lebesgue
measurable ([[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]]). In
particular every open set, every closed set and every countable intersection of
open sets is Lebesgue measurable.

Let $n \ge 1$ and **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]). Then:

1. $\mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a sigma-algebra on $\mathbb{R}^n$ and
   $\lambda_n$ is a measure on it ([[def-measure]]);
2. the measure space $(\mathbb{R}^n, \mathcal{L}(\mathbb{R}^n), \lambda_n)$ is
   complete ([[def-complete-measure-space]]), and every $S \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$
   with $\lambda_n^*(S) = 0$ is Lebesgue measurable with $\lambda_n(S) = 0$;
3. every elementary set is Lebesgue measurable and
   $\lambda_n(A) = \mu_0(A)$ for every $A \in \mathcal{E}_n$; in particular
   $\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ for every half-open box $B$,
   $\lambda_n(\varnothing) = 0$ and $\lambda_n(\mathbb{R}^n) = +\infty$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Let $n \ge 1$, **assume the Axiom of Countable Choice**
([[def-countable-choice]]), and let $a_i \le b_i$ be reals for $i<n$. Write

$$R^{\circ} := \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i < x_i < b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}, \qquad \overline{R} := [a,b] = \{\, x \in \mathbb{R}^n : a_i \le x_i \le b_i \text{ for every } i<n \,\}$$

([[def-multidimensional-rectangle-and-volume]]). Then $R^{\circ}$ is open and
$\overline{R}$ is closed, so both are Borel and Lebesgue measurable, and **every**
set $R$ with $R^{\circ} \subseteq R \subseteq \overline{R}$ is Lebesgue
measurable with

$$\lambda_n(R) \;=\; \prod_{i<n}(b_i-a_i).$$

In particular this covers the four one-dimensional face conventions in each
coordinate — the open box, the closed box $[a,b]$, the half-open box
$B(a,b) = \prod_{i<n}(a_i,b_i]$ of [[def-half-open-box]], and every mixture of
them, in any combination of coordinates — and it gives measure $0$ to all of them
whenever $a_i = b_i$ for some $i<n$. For a half-open box with infinite
parameters the value is already
$\lambda_n(B) = \operatorname{vol}(B)$ ([[thm-lebesgue-measure-is-a-complete-measure]]).

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces. Then:

1. the set function $E \mapsto (\mu \times \nu)(E)$ of
   [[def-product-measure-on-sigma-finite-spaces]] is a measure on
   $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$;
2. for measurable rectangles,
   $$(\mu \times \nu)(A \times B)=\mu(A)\nu(B),$$
   with the nonnegative extended-product convention $0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0$;
3. the measure $\mu \times \nu$ is sigma-finite; and
4. it is the unique measure on $\mathcal A \otimes \mathcal B$ with the
   rectangle formula.

Let $(\mu_k)$ be measures on one measurable space and let $c_k\in[0,+\infty]$. Each scalar multiple $c_k\mu_k$, defined by the zero, finite-positive, and positive-infinity branches of [[def-nonnegative-weighted-sum-of-measures]], is a measure. Every finite or countable weighted sum $\sum_kc_k\mu_k$ is also a measure.

Let $S$ be as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. A
**Poisson point process with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure
$\nu$** is a point process $\eta$ such that for every finite pairwise-disjoint
family of Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_m$, the counts $\eta(B_i)$ are independent
random elements ([[def-independent-random-elements]]) and $\eta(B_i)$ has the
scalar Poisson law of mean $\nu(B_i)$
([[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]],
[[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]). If $\nu(B)=\infty$,
the extended count convention is $\eta(B)=+\infty$ almost surely.
Here sigma-finite means that $S$ is a countable union of Borel sets of finite
$\nu$-measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]); for the
stated $S$, local finiteness also implies sigma-finiteness by the compact
exhaustion in
[[lem-locally-compact-second-countable-spaces-have-compact-exhaustions]].

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the evaluation-measurable space of locally
finite Borel measures. A **Cox point process directed by a random measure
$\xi$** consists of a point process $\eta$, a random locally finite measure
$\xi$, and a supplied probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$
to $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ such that $K(\xi,\cdot)$ is a regular
conditional law of $\eta$ given $\xi$
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]) and, for $P_\xi$-almost every
$\mu$, $K(\mu,\cdot)$ is the law of a Poisson point process of intensity
$\mu$. The kernel is part of the model data; this definition does not assert
that such a kernel exists for every $(\eta,\xi)$. The mean measure of $\xi$ is
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, a measure by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]].

Both definitions permit multiplicities. They do not assert that diffuse
directing measures yield simple processes or that a Cox law determines the law
of its directing measure.

Let $\mathcal A$ be a sigma-algebra on a nonempty set $X$ ([[def-sigma-algebra]]) and fix $x_0\in X$. The **Dirac set function at $x_0$** is

$$\delta_{x_0}(E):=\begin{cases}1,&x_0\in E,\\0,&x_0\notin E,\end{cases}\qquad E\in\mathcal A.$$

The two branches are exhaustive and disjoint. The fact that this set function is a probability measure is proved in [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]].
For $x_0\in X$, the Dirac set function $\delta_{x_0}$ is a probability measure on every sigma-algebra on $X$.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ and $(Y,\mathcal B,\nu)$ be sigma-finite measure
spaces, and let $f : X \times Y \to [0,\infty]$ be product-measurable. Then
$x \mapsto \int_Y f_x\,d\nu$ and $y \mapsto \int_X f^y\,d\mu$ are measurable,
and

$$\int_{X \times Y} f\,d(\mu \times \nu) = \int_X \left(\int_Y f_x\,d\nu\right)d\mu = \int_Y \left(\int_X f^y\,d\mu\right)d\nu.$$

Fix a locally compact, second-countable Hausdorff topological space $S$
([[def-locally-compact-space]], [[def-second-countable-space]],
[[def-hausdorff-space]]). Here locally compact means that every point has a
compact neighbourhood; second countable means that the topology has an at most
countable basis; and Hausdorff means that distinct points have disjoint open
neighbourhoods. Let $\mathcal B(S)$ be the Borel sigma-algebra generated by the
open sets ([[def-borel-sigma-algebra]]).

A **counting measure** on $S$ is a Borel measure of the form
$\mu=\sum_{j\in J}\delta_{x_j}$ for a finite or countable index set $J$ and
points $x_j\in S$, where repetitions are allowed and the empty sum is zero.
Each $\delta_x$ is the unit point mass at $x$
([[def-dirac-measure]], [[prop-dirac-measure-is-a-probability-measure]]), and
the countable sum is a measure by
[[thm-nonnegative-weighted-sums-of-measures]]. The **multiplicity** at $x$ is
$\mu(\{x\})$. The counting measure is **locally finite** if
$\mu(K)<\infty$ for every compact subset $K\subseteq S$
([[def-compact-space]]).

Let $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of locally finite counting
measures, equipped with the sigma-algebra generated by the **evaluation maps**
$\mu\mapsto\mu(B)$ for $B\in\mathcal B(S)$. A **point process** on $S$ is a
measurable map $\eta:(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)\to
(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$ from a probability space
([[def-probability-measure]]), with measurability in the sense of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Equivalently, every
count $\eta(B)$ is a measurable random variable, because the evaluation maps
generate $\mathcal E$. Its **law** is the probability measure
$\mathbb P_\eta(A)=\mathbb P(\eta^{-1}(A))$ on $(\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S),\mathcal E)$
([[def-law-or-distribution-of-a-random-element]],
[[lem-law-of-a-random-element-is-a-probability-measure]]). The process is
classified by its realized configurations: a configuration $\mu$ is
**simple** if $\mu(\{x\})\le1$ for every $x$, and is **multiplicity-bearing**
if some singleton has mass greater than one. This is a pointwise distinction;
no almost-sure simplicity assertion is part of this definition.

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the set of all locally finite Borel
measures on $S$, with the sigma-algebra generated by their evaluation maps. A
**random locally finite measure** $\xi$ is a measurable map into this space.

For a nonnegative Borel function $f$, write
$\eta(f):=\int_S f\,d\eta$. Define the expected measure, or **intensity
measure**, by $\nu(B):=\mathbb E[\eta(B)]$. The expected-measure and
random-integral measurability assertions are justified by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]]. The measure
$\nu$ need not be locally finite; it is locally finite exactly when
$\mathbb E[\eta(K)]<\infty$ for each compact $K$.

The mean measure of a random locally finite measure is likewise
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, covered by the same expected-measure lemma. Local
finiteness of each realization does not by itself assert local finiteness of
$\nu$.

derivations.claim: Put $\lambda=\theta T$ and let $Q=\ell/T$, a probability measure on $S$ by [A1] and [F2]. For each $n\ge0$, use the finite product probability $Q^{\otimes n}$ on $S^n$; for $n=0$, $S^0$ is the singleton empty tuple with unit mass. Form the countable disjoint union $\Omega=\coprod_{n\ge0}(\{n\}\times S^n)$ with the sigma-algebra whose sections in each component are product-measurable. Put $p_n=e^{-\lambda}\lambda^n/n!$ and define $P(E)=\sum_{n\ge0}p_nQ^{\otimes n}(E_n)$. [F1] gives $\sum_np_n=1$; [F4] makes $P$ a probability measure. On component $n$, set $\eta=\sum_{i=1}^n\delta_{x_i}$. Every evaluation $\eta(B)=\sum_{i=1}^n1_B(x_i)$ is measurable, and each realization has at most $n$ atoms, so it is locally finite. The space $S$ is locally compact, second countable, and Hausdorff by the displayed neighborhood and base checks; hence [F8] makes $\eta$ a point process.

Let $B_1,\ldots,B_r$ be disjoint Borel subsets of $S$, put $B_0=S\setminus\bigcup_{j=1}^rB_j$, and set $q_j=Q(B_j)$. Conditional on component $n$, a count vector $(k_0,\ldots,k_r)$ with sum $n$ occurs for $n!/\prod_{j=0}^r k_j!$ coordinate assignments; each assignment has probability $\prod_{j=0}^r q_j^{k_j}$ by [F3]. Multiplying by $p_n$ and summing over $k_0\ge0$ gives, for fixed $k_1,\ldots,k_r\in\mathbb N_0$, $P\{\eta(B_j)=k_j,\ 1\le j\le r\}=\sum_{k_0=0}^\infty e^{-\lambda}\frac{(\lambda q_0)^{k_0}}{k_0!}\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(\lambda q_j)^{k_j}}{k_j!}=e^{-\lambda}\prod_{j=1}^r\frac{(\lambda q_j)^{k_j}}{k_j!}\sum_{k_0=0}^\infty\frac{(\lambda q_0)^{k_0}}{k_0!}=\prod_{j=1}^r\left[e^{-\lambda q_j}\frac{(\lambda q_j)^{k_j}}{k_j!}\right].$ Here $0^0=1$ for zero-mass cells, and $q_0=1-\sum_{j=1}^rq_j$. The exponential series evaluates the sum, and $\lambda q_j=\theta\ell(B_j)$. Thus the joint count mass factors into the independent Poisson masses with means $\nu_\theta(B_j)$; [F5] makes $\eta$ a Poisson point process of intensity $\nu_\theta$.

Conditional on component $n$, the coordinate vector has density $T^{-n}$ on $S^n$. For each pair $i<j$, the diagonal $\{x_i=x_j\}$ is Borel; its section in coordinate $x_j$ is a singleton and has Lebesgue measure zero by [F2], so [F7] gives product measure zero. The finite union of pairwise diagonals is null. Coordinate permutations preserve the product-uniform law: they preserve the rectangle formula in [F3], and uniqueness there extends that equality from rectangles to the product sigma-algebra. Thus the $n!$ ordering regions have equal measure and partition the cube outside the diagonals. More precisely, for every Borel $C\subseteq\Delta_n$, the preimage of $C$ under the Borel sorting map, off the diagonals, is the disjoint union of the $n!$ coordinate permutations of $C$. Each has product-uniform probability $T^{-n}\ell^n(C)$, so sorting gives conditional density $n!/T^n$ on the ordered simplex. Multiplying by $p_n=e^{-\theta T}(\theta T)^n/n!$ gives joint density $e^{-\theta T}\theta^n$. The endpoint set where any coordinate equals $T$ has product measure zero because $Q(\{T\})=0$ by [F2] and [F3]; thus the same density applies to the stated simplex with $t_n\le T$. For $n=0$, the construction gives empty-pattern mass $p_0=e^{-\theta T}$. Each component has tie probability zero, and their countable mixture also has tie probability zero. This proves the event-time density and simplicity claims.

citations.quote:
Assume the Axiom of Choice as in
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. Fix a finite
horizon $T>0$, a probability space with an increasing filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]], and an adapted
càdlàg (right-continuous with left limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued
process $N$ with $N_0=0$, $N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and jumps
$\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ outside one null event. Such a process is **simple**:
its event times are strictly ordered,
$0<T_1<\cdots<T_{N_T}\le T$. It is **locally finite** when it has finitely
many events on every finite interval.

For conditional-law calculations, the model supplies a measurable history
space $(\mathsf H,\mathcal G)$, an adapted measurable history random element
$H_t$ recording the initial information and events observed through time $t$,
and a measurable update map $h\mapsto h\oplus u$ that appends an event at
time $u$. Write $\mathcal H_t:=\sigma(H_t)$ and let $H_{t-}$ record only
events strictly before $t$. Relevant exogenous covariates are included in
the supplied history. Measurability has the meaning of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Predictability is
measurability for the predictable sigma-algebra generated by
$(s,u]\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$ and the time-zero generators, as in
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]].

The model supplies a probability kernel $K_{t,h}$ on $(t,\infty]$ for the
next event time given history $h$ at time $t$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]],
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]); its finite-time density
versions are jointly measurable in $(t,h,u)$. The value $+\infty$ means that
no later event occurs. If the finite-time measure is absolutely continuous
with respect to Lebesgue measure
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]],
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), let $f_{t,h}$ be its supplied
nonnegative Radon--Nikodym density
([[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]). Write
$S_{t,h}(u):=K_{t,h}((u,\infty])$ for its survivor and define its
**no-event conditional hazard** by
$$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u):=\frac{f_{t,h}(u)}{S_{t,h}(u)}\qquad\text{where }S_{t,h}(u)>0.$$
Assume these hazards are locally integrable on every finite interval. The
model also supplies a nonnegative predictable effective-intensity process
$\lambda^*$ compatible with these waiting-time hazards: for each history
$h$ at time $t$, on its supplied measurable no-event continuation up to
$u>t$, the pre-event intensity $\lambda^*(u\mid h_{u-})$ agrees with
$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u)$ for Lebesgue-almost every $u$. The jointly measurable
hazard representatives used in the event-density factors are these same
versions on their proper domains $u>t$. Compatibility with the predictable
process is a model requirement, not an evaluation of a waiting-time density
at its excluded left endpoint. This pre-event convention means the event
at $u$ does not change its own intensity.

The **temporal conditional-intensity model** requires both this
hazard-compatible conditional law and the separate counting-process
compensator contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]: if an at-risk
indicator $Y$ and intensity density $\lambda$ are separately specified, the
effective intensity is $\lambda^*=Y\lambda$; without an at-risk indicator,
it is $\lambda^*$. Then $A_t=\int_0^t\lambda^*(u)\,du$ is finite pathwise,
continuous, adapted and predictable, $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$, and $N-A$ is
a square-integrable martingale in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. At-risk exposure, if
present, is part of the effective intensity. The compensator clause is a
model assumption: a displayed hazard formula alone proves neither that a
process with this law exists nor that the martingale contract holds. No
stationarity or non-explosion claim follows from writing an intensity
specification.

Fix a supplied event history $h$ at time $t$ in the model of
[[def-temporal-point-process-and-conditional-intensity]]. Let
$\lambda_h^*(u)$ be its nonnegative no-event conditional hazard, supplied as
a locally integrable version on every finite interval, and put
$$\Lambda_h(u):=\int_t^u\lambda_h^*(s)\,ds.$$
For each finite $U>t$, on $t\le u\le U$ the conditional survivor and finite-
time density of the next event are
$$S_h(u)=\exp(-\Lambda_h(u)),\qquad f_h(u)=\lambda_h^*(u)\exp(-\Lambda_h(u))\quad\text{for almost every }u.$$
If $\Lambda_h(u)\to\Lambda_h(\infty)<\infty$ as $u\to\infty$, then
$K_h(\{\infty\})=\exp(-\Lambda_h(\infty))$. If
$\Lambda_h(u)\to\infty$, this terminal mass is zero. These conclusions
concern one next-event law and do not prove non-explosion of an entire
process.

Let $T>0$, $\theta>0$, and let $S=(0,T]$ carry its subspace topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. This space is Hausdorff as a subspace of $\mathbb R$;
rational intervals give a countable base; and each $x\in S$ has a compact
neighborhood $[x-\delta,x+\delta]\cap S$ for some $0<\delta<x$. Let $\ell$
be Lebesgue measure restricted to $S$. There exists a Poisson point process
on $S$ with intensity measure $\nu_\theta(B)=\theta\ell(B)$. Its total
count is finite almost surely, its event times have no ties almost surely,
and for every integer $m\ge0$ the joint density of the ordered event times
$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$
with respect to $m$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the ordered simplex is
$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$
For $m>0$, conditional on $N(S)=m$, the ordered event times have density
$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

Let $P_0$ and $P_1$ be probability measures on the same measurable space.
Assume AC. Their Lebesgue decomposition relative to $P_0$ is the unique
decomposition
$P_1=P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}+P_{1,\mathrm{s}}$ with
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}\ll P_0$ and $P_{1,\mathrm{s}}\perp P_0$
([[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-exists-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]],
[[thm-lebesgue-decomposition-is-unique-for-sigma-finite-signed-measures]]).
Both components are positive by
[[lem-positive-lebesgue-components-of-a-positive-measure]], and
$P_{1,\mathrm{ac}}$ is finite because their sum has mass one. Define the
**likelihood-ratio density** of $P_1$ against $P_0$ to be the
$P_0$-almost-everywhere class
$$
\frac{dP_{1,\mathrm{ac}}}{dP_0}
$$
of [[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]. Under AC this class has a nonnegative
measurable representative by
[[lem-radon-nikodym-density-of-a-finite-positive-measure-has-a-nonnegative-representative]].

This is a full density of $P_1$ with respect to $P_0$ only in the
absolutely continuous case $P_1\ll P_0$. If that condition fails, the
singular component remains separate. A displayed representative is not a
canonical pointwise function: its values are determined only
$P_0$-almost everywhere.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$.
Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when

$$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$

The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following
statement.

> For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every
> $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]],
> [[def-natural-numbers]]) with
> $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$

Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily
a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is
indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every
later term is related to its predecessor.

**What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and
[[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is
fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed
by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made. DC is
the principle needed when the $n$-th set to select from is not known until the
first $n$ selections have been made: here the admissible values of $x_{n+1}$ are
exactly the $R$-successors of $x_n$, so the family being chosen from is built
along the choosing. Thus the displayed recursion is directly an instance of
DC; it is not itself an application of the fixed-family formulation of
countable choice. This observation concerns the input to the two axioms and
makes no claim about a nonimplication between them.

**The starting point may be dropped.** The formally weaker statement obtained by
deleting the clause $x_0 = a$ — for every nonempty $X$ and every entire $R$ there
is a sequence with $x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ for all $n$ — is an immediate
consequence of the form above, since $X$ is nonempty and any of its elements may
be taken as $a$. Conversely, assume the start-free form, and fix $X$, $R$ and $a$ as above. Let $P$ be the set of all functions $p:k\to X$ with nonzero $k\in\mathbb N$, $p(0)=a$, and $p(i)\mathbin R p(i+1)$ whenever $i+1<k$. It is a set by Separation inside $\mathcal P(\mathbb N\times X)$ ([[def-power-set]], [[def-cartesian-product]], [[def-axiom-schema-of-separation]]); a natural is the set of its predecessors ([[lem-nat-order-is-membership]]). The singleton path $\{(0,a)\}$ lies in $P$.

On $P$ let $p\mathbin S q$ mean that $q$ extends $p$ by exactly one new last entry. This relation is entire: for one particular $p:k\to X$, write $k=j+1$ ([[lem-nat-nonzero-is-successor]]); an $R$-successor $y$ of $p(j)$ exists, and $q=p\cup\{(k,y)\}$ is the required extension. This is existential instantiation for that path, not a simultaneous choice of successors. Start-free DC now supplies a sequence $(p_n)$ with $p_n\mathbin S p_{n+1}$; its first path need not be the singleton path, but every path in $P$ already starts at $a$.

Their graphs are nested. By induction ([[thm-induction-principle]]), $p_n$ has at least $n+1$ entries: the initial path is nonempty, and every step adds one entry. Hence $x=\bigcup_{n\in\mathbb N}p_n$ is a function with domain $\mathbb N$ and values in $X$. Indeed, nestedness makes all common values agree, every natural index eventually lies in a path, and no path has indices outside $\mathbb N$. Each path starts at $a$, so $x(0)=a$; for any $i$, a sufficiently long path contains both $i$ and $i+1$, giving $x(i)\mathbin R x(i+1)$. Replacement and Union form this union of the sequence of graphs. Thus the start-free and prescribed-start forms are equivalent in ZF. Every use below retains the prescribed-start convention.

**$R$ need not be an order and the terms need not be distinct.** What DC delivers
is a sequence, that is a function $\mathbb{N} \to X$, not a chain in the
order-theoretic sense ([[def-chain]]). The relation may be symmetric, and the
sequence may repeat a value or be constant; all that is asserted is
$x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1}$ at every index.

derivations.claim: For $m\ge1$, recursively define the density of the first $i$ event times by $g_0=1$ and $g_i(t_1,\ldots,t_i)=g_{i-1}(t_1,\ldots,t_{i-1}) f_\theta(t_i\mid h_{i-1})$ on the ordered prefix simplex. At $i=1$ this is the supplied conditional density. If the first $i-1$ times have density $g_{i-1}$, conditioning on that prefix and integrating its supplied probability kernel for the next waiting time multiplies the density by $f_\theta(t_i\mid h_{i-1})$; iterated kernel integration proves the formula for $i$. The measurable update and kernel assumptions in [F1] make each factor measurable. For exactly $m$ events by $T$, the final history must have no event in $(t_m,T]$, whose conditional probability is $S_\theta(T\mid h_m)$. Thus the pattern density is $\prod_{i=1}^mf_\theta(t_i\mid h_{i-1})S_\theta(T\mid h_m)$; for $m=0$ it is the initial no-event probability. The simplices exhaust the pattern space because the event count is finite almost surely.

By [F2], each event-time density is its pre-event intensity times $\exp\!\left(-\int_{t_{i-1}}^{t_i}\lambda_\theta^*(u\mid h_{u-})\,du\right)$, where $t_0=0$, and the terminal survivor is $\exp(-\int_{t_m}^{T}\lambda_\theta^*(u\mid h_{u-})\,du)$. Multiplying these terms adds the integrals over the adjacent intervals $(0,t_1],\ldots,(t_m,T]$, so on $\Delta_m$ the pattern density is $p_\theta(t_1,\ldots,t_m)=\left(\prod_{i=1}^m\lambda_\theta^*(t_i\mid h_{i-1})\right)\exp\!\left(-\int_0^T\lambda_\theta^*(u\mid h_{u-})\,du\right)$. For $m=0$ there are no event factors and the same expression uses the empty product.

By [F3], the reference density equals $e^{-T}>0$ on each $\Delta_m$ and its empty-pattern mass is positive. If a measurable set in $\mathsf X_T$ has $P_0$-measure zero, its section in every $\Delta_m$ is Lebesgue-null and it excludes the empty pattern. Step 2.1 gives a Lebesgue density for $P_\theta$ on every simplex, so each section has $P_\theta$-measure zero; countable additivity over the disjoint union gives $P_\theta\ll P_0$. By [F4], the Radon–Nikodym derivative is the ratio of the two pattern densities, namely $p_\theta/e^{-T}=e^Tp_\theta$, $P_0$-almost everywhere. If any factor at an observed event is zero, this representative is zero; when all are positive, taking logarithms and discarding the parameter-free term $T$ gives the stated likelihood form.

Let $S$ be as in [[def-random-measure-and-locally-finite-point-process]]. A
**Poisson point process with locally finite, sigma-finite intensity measure
$\nu$** is a point process $\eta$ such that for every finite pairwise-disjoint
family of Borel sets $B_1,\ldots,B_m$, the counts $\eta(B_i)$ are independent
random elements ([[def-independent-random-elements]]) and $\eta(B_i)$ has the
scalar Poisson law of mean $\nu(B_i)$
([[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]],
[[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]). If $\nu(B)=\infty$,
the extended count convention is $\eta(B)=+\infty$ almost surely.
Here sigma-finite means that $S$ is a countable union of Borel sets of finite
$\nu$-measure ([[def-finite-sigma-finite-and-semifinite-measures]]); for the
stated $S$, local finiteness also implies sigma-finiteness by the compact
exhaustion in
[[lem-locally-compact-second-countable-spaces-have-compact-exhaustions]].

Let $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ be the evaluation-measurable space of locally
finite Borel measures. A **Cox point process directed by a random measure
$\xi$** consists of a point process $\eta$, a random locally finite measure
$\xi$, and a supplied probability kernel $K$ from $\mathcal M_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$
to $\mathcal N_{\mathrm{lf}}(S)$ such that $K(\xi,\cdot)$ is a regular
conditional law of $\eta$ given $\xi$
([[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]) and, for $P_\xi$-almost every
$\mu$, $K(\mu,\cdot)$ is the law of a Poisson point process of intensity
$\mu$. The kernel is part of the model data; this definition does not assert
that such a kernel exists for every $(\eta,\xi)$. The mean measure of $\xi$ is
$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, a measure by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]].

Both definitions permit multiplicities. They do not assert that diffuse
directing measures yield simple processes or that a Cox law determines the law
of its directing measure.

Let $T>0$, $\theta>0$, and let $S=(0,T]$ carry its subspace topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. This space is Hausdorff as a subspace of $\mathbb R$;
rational intervals give a countable base; and each $x\in S$ has a compact
neighborhood $[x-\delta,x+\delta]\cap S$ for some $0<\delta<x$. Let $\ell$
be Lebesgue measure restricted to $S$. There exists a Poisson point process
on $S$ with intensity measure $\nu_\theta(B)=\theta\ell(B)$. Its total
count is finite almost surely, its event times have no ties almost surely,
and for every integer $m\ge0$ the joint density of the ordered event times
$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$
with respect to $m$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the ordered simplex is
$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$
For $m>0$, conditional on $N(S)=m$, the ordered event times have density
$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Let $(\Pi_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of pi-systems in a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and assume $\Omega\in\Pi_i$ for every $i$.
If the family $(\Pi_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent, then the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(\Pi_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires that this integral
be finite pathwise, that $A$ be continuous, adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

Fix a supplied event history $h$ at time $t$ in the model of
[[def-temporal-point-process-and-conditional-intensity]]. Let
$\lambda_h^*(u)$ be its nonnegative no-event conditional hazard, supplied as
a locally integrable version on every finite interval, and put
$$\Lambda_h(u):=\int_t^u\lambda_h^*(s)\,ds.$$
For each finite $U>t$, on $t\le u\le U$ the conditional survivor and finite-
time density of the next event are
$$S_h(u)=\exp(-\Lambda_h(u)),\qquad f_h(u)=\lambda_h^*(u)\exp(-\Lambda_h(u))\quad\text{for almost every }u.$$
If $\Lambda_h(u)\to\Lambda_h(\infty)<\infty$ as $u\to\infty$, then
$K_h(\{\infty\})=\exp(-\Lambda_h(\infty))$. If
$\Lambda_h(u)\to\infty$, this terminal mass is zero. These conclusions
concern one next-event law and do not prove non-explosion of an entire
process.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. Fix a finite
horizon $T>0$, a probability space with an increasing filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]], and an adapted
càdlàg (right-continuous with left limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued
process $N$ with $N_0=0$, $N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and jumps
$\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ outside one null event. Such a process is **simple**:
its event times are strictly ordered,
$0<T_1<\cdots<T_{N_T}\le T$. It is **locally finite** when it has finitely
many events on every finite interval.

For conditional-law calculations, the model supplies a measurable history
space $(\mathsf H,\mathcal G)$, an adapted measurable history random element
$H_t$ recording the initial information and events observed through time $t$,
and a measurable update map $h\mapsto h\oplus u$ that appends an event at
time $u$. Write $\mathcal H_t:=\sigma(H_t)$ and let $H_{t-}$ record only
events strictly before $t$. Relevant exogenous covariates are included in
the supplied history. Measurability has the meaning of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Predictability is
measurability for the predictable sigma-algebra generated by
$(s,u]\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$ and the time-zero generators, as in
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]].

The model supplies a probability kernel $K_{t,h}$ on $(t,\infty]$ for the
next event time given history $h$ at time $t$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]],
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]); its finite-time density
versions are jointly measurable in $(t,h,u)$. The value $+\infty$ means that
no later event occurs. If the finite-time measure is absolutely continuous
with respect to Lebesgue measure
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]],
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), let $f_{t,h}$ be its supplied
nonnegative Radon--Nikodym density
([[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]). Write
$S_{t,h}(u):=K_{t,h}((u,\infty])$ for its survivor and define its
**no-event conditional hazard** by
$$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u):=\frac{f_{t,h}(u)}{S_{t,h}(u)}\qquad\text{where }S_{t,h}(u)>0.$$
Assume these hazards are locally integrable on every finite interval. The
model also supplies a nonnegative predictable effective-intensity process
$\lambda^*$ compatible with these waiting-time hazards: for each history
$h$ at time $t$, on its supplied measurable no-event continuation up to
$u>t$, the pre-event intensity $\lambda^*(u\mid h_{u-})$ agrees with
$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u)$ for Lebesgue-almost every $u$. The jointly measurable
hazard representatives used in the event-density factors are these same
versions on their proper domains $u>t$. Compatibility with the predictable
process is a model requirement, not an evaluation of a waiting-time density
at its excluded left endpoint. This pre-event convention means the event
at $u$ does not change its own intensity.

The **temporal conditional-intensity model** requires both this
hazard-compatible conditional law and the separate counting-process
compensator contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]: if an at-risk
indicator $Y$ and intensity density $\lambda$ are separately specified, the
effective intensity is $\lambda^*=Y\lambda$; without an at-risk indicator,
it is $\lambda^*$. Then $A_t=\int_0^t\lambda^*(u)\,du$ is finite pathwise,
continuous, adapted and predictable, $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$, and $N-A$ is
a square-integrable martingale in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. At-risk exposure, if
present, is part of the effective intensity. The compensator clause is a
model assumption: a displayed hazard formula alone proves neither that a
process with this law exists nor that the martingale contract holds. No
stationarity or non-explosion claim follows from writing an intensity
specification.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

Define the history random element by $H_s(B):=\eta(B\cap(0,s\wedge1])$ for every Borel $B\subseteq(0,\infty)$. For $0\le s\le t$, the increment $N_t-N_s$ is the count on $(s,t]\cap(0,1]$, a Poisson variable of mean $\min(t,1)-\min(s,1)$. Refine a finite family of past Borel sets into the disjoint atoms of the finite Boolean algebra they generate. Every atom lies in $(0,s]$, so [F1] gives independence of its count vector from the future increment. These count cylinders generate the natural-history sigma-algebra, and [F5] extends independence to that sigma-algebra. Therefore $\mathbb E[N_t-N_s\mid\mathcal H_s]=\min(t,1)-\min(s,1)=A_t-A_s$. Thus $N-A$ is a martingale. Since $N_t$ has finite second moment by [F3] and $A_t\le1$, this martingale is square-integrable and meets [F6]; $\mathbb E[A_T]\le1$.

For $s\ge0$ and $h\in\mathsf H$, supply the next-event kernel, viewed on $[0,\infty]$ and supported on $(s,\infty]$, by $$K_{s,h}(C):=\int_{C\cap(s,1]}e^{-(u-s)}\,du+e^{-(1-s)_+}\mathbf1_{\{\infty\in C\}}$$ for Borel $C\subseteq[0,\infty]$, where $x_+:=\max(x,0)$. Its finite-time mass is $1-e^{-(1-s)_+}$, so each $K_{s,h}$ is a probability measure. For fixed $C$, the finite-time term is $e^s\int_{C\cap(s,1]}e^{-u}\,du$, a Borel function of $s$ because the tail integral is monotone on $[0,1]$ and zero for $s\ge1$; the atom mass is also Borel. The finite-time density $f_{s,h}(u)=\mathbf1_{\{s<u\le1\}}e^{-(u-s)}$ is jointly measurable in $(s,h,u)$. By independent future increments, this is the conditional next-event law given $H_s$: its survivor for $u>s$ is $S_{s,h}(u)=e^{-((u\wedge1)-s)_+}$, since the event of no point in $(s,u]\cap(0,1]$ has probability $e^{-((u\wedge1)-s)_+}$. Taking $u\to\infty$ in step 3.1 gives $\Pr(T_1=\infty)=e^{-1}$, also the zero-count probability $\Pr(N_1=0)$ by [F3]. No events occur after time $1$, and $N_1$ is finite almost surely, so the process terminates and is non-explosive.
