$\nu(B)=\mathbb E[\xi(B)]$, a measure by
[[lem-mean-measure-and-integrals-of-a-random-point-process]].

Both definitions permit multiplicities. They do not assert that diffuse
directing measures yield simple processes or that a Cox law determines the law
of its directing measure.

Let $T>0$, $\theta>0$, and let $S=(0,T]$ carry its subspace topology and
Borel sigma-algebra. This space is Hausdorff as a subspace of $\mathbb R$;
rational intervals give a countable base; and each $x\in S$ has a compact
neighborhood $[x-\delta,x+\delta]\cap S$ for some $0<\delta<x$. Let $\ell$
be Lebesgue measure restricted to $S$. There exists a Poisson point process
on $S$ with intensity measure $\nu_\theta(B)=\theta\ell(B)$. Its total
count is finite almost surely, its event times have no ties almost surely,
and for every integer $m\ge0$ the joint density of the ordered event times
$$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T,\qquad N(S)=m,$$
with respect to $m$-dimensional Lebesgue measure on the ordered simplex is
$$e^{-\theta T}\theta^m.$$
For $m>0$, conditional on $N(S)=m$, the ordered event times have density
$m!/T^m$. For $m=0$ the empty-pattern probability is $e^{-\theta T}$.

For a finite parameter $\lambda\ge0$, the **Poisson count law**
$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$ is the probability measure on
$\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ whose masses are
$$\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)\{k\}=e^{-\lambda}\frac{\lambda^k}{k!},\qquad k\in\mathbb N_0,$$
when $\lambda>0$, and is the point mass at $0$ when $\lambda=0$. The
normalization and the moment and generating-function identities used below are
proved in [[lem-poisson-count-law-normalization-and-moments]]. The separate
extended convention for a point-process count on a Borel set of infinite
intensity is that the count equals $+\infty$ almost surely; it is not a finite
Poisson probability law.

For finite $\lambda\ge0$, the masses in
[[def-scalar-poisson-count-law]] sum to one. If $N\sim\operatorname{Pois}(\lambda)$,
then
$$\mathbb E[N]=\lambda,\qquad \mathbb E[N(N-1)]=\lambda^2,\qquad \mathbb E[N^2]=\lambda^2+\lambda,\qquad \operatorname{Var}(N)=\lambda,$$
and $\mathbb E[s^N]=\exp(\lambda(s-1))$ for $0\le s\le1$.

Let $(\Pi_i)_{i\in I}$ be a family of pi-systems in a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,\mathbb P)$, and assume $\Omega\in\Pi_i$ for every $i$.
If the family $(\Pi_i)_{i\in I}$ is independent, then the sigma-algebras
$(\sigma(\Pi_i))_{i\in I}$ are independent.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Let
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space with a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. All processes here
are real-valued and indexed by $[0,\infty)$. AC is inherited from the cited
continuous-time-filtration interface, whose separate martingale clause uses
conditional expectation. Once the filtered probability space and stopping
times are given, the progressive and predictable constructions below make no
additional choice: they use only generated sigma-algebras and product
rectangles.

1. **Progressively measurable.** A process $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **progressively measurable** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when for every
   $t\ge0$ the restricted map
   $[0,t]\times\Omega\to\mathbb R$, $(s,\omega)\mapsto X_s(\omega)$, is
   measurable for the product sigma-algebra
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$
   [[def-product-sigma-algebra-and-finite-product-sigma-algebras]].

2. **Time-zero and interval generators.** On the product space
   $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$, let $\mathcal P$ be the sigma-algebra generated by
   the family
   $$\mathcal G:=\bigl\{(s,u]\times A:\ 0\le s<u<\infty,\ A\in\mathcal F_s\bigr\}\ \cup\ \bigl\{\{0\}\times A:\ A\in\mathcal F_0\bigr\}.$$
   The interval generators with $s=0$ are included, so $(0,u]\times A$ with
   $A\in\mathcal F_0$ is a generator. The sigma-algebra $\mathcal P$ exists by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]] and is called the
   **predictable sigma-algebra**. A process $H=(H_t)_{t\ge0}$ is
   **predictable** when the map $(s,\omega)\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is
   $\mathcal P$-measurable. For a finite horizon $T>0$ we write
   $\mathcal P_T$ for the sigma-algebra on $[0,T]\times\Omega$ generated by the
   same family restricted to $u\le T$ together with the time-zero generators;
   this is the trace of $\mathcal P$ on $[0,T]\times\Omega$. Indeed, the
   trace of an interval generator is empty when $s\ge T$, and otherwise is
   $(s,\min(u,T)]\times A$, while time-zero generators are unchanged.
   Conversely every listed finite-horizon generator is such a trace.

3. **Sections, adaptedness, and null sets.** Two structural conventions are
   used repeatedly and are part of the definition.
   (a) Every generator is a measurable rectangle of
   $\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$, hence
   $\mathcal P\subseteq\mathcal B([0,\infty))\otimes\mathcal F$; the time-zero
   generator $\{0\}\times A$ has $dt\otimes P$-measure zero for every $A$. A
   set in $\mathcal P$ has its section at each fixed time $s$ in $\mathcal F_s$:
   sets with that section property form a sigma-algebra, and each generator
   has the property by the increasing-filtration condition. Its section at
   each fixed $\omega$ is Borel in time, by the same sigma-algebra argument.
   (b) If a process is predictable then it is progressively measurable: for
   $s\le t$ the section $\omega\mapsto H_s(\omega)$ is $\mathcal F_s$-measurable
   $\subseteq\mathcal F_t$-measurable, and the progressive-measurability claim
   is the restriction of the joint map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$; the restriction
   of a $\mathcal P$-measurable map to $[0,t]\times\Omega$ is measurable for
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$ because every generator with $u\le t$
   lies in that product sigma-algebra and the generators with $u>t$ have
   intersection with $[0,t]\times\Omega$ of the form $(s,t]\times A$ with
   $s<t$ and $A\in\mathcal F_s$, or the empty set when $s\ge t$.
   The time-zero generators also lie in
   $\mathcal B([0,t])\otimes\mathcal F_t$.

The family $\mathcal G$ need not itself contain the whole space, but a finite intersection
of generators is empty or again a generator, or a time-zero generator, because
$(s,u]\cap(s',u']=(s\vee s',u\wedge u']$ and $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_{s\vee s'}$
whenever $A\in\mathcal F_s$, $A'\in\mathcal F_{s'}$, while
$\{0\}\times A$ is disjoint from every interval generator, including
$(0,u]\times A'$. Two time-zero generators intersect in
$\{0\}\times(A\cap A')$ with $A\cap A'\in\mathcal F_0$.
Thus the family consisting of the whole space
together with finite intersections of generators is a pi-system generating
$\mathcal P$; this is the structural fact used by the density theorem below.

Because predictability is a measurability requirement for the joint map, it is
preserved by pointwise limits, products and linear combinations of predictable
processes. A deterministic function $h$ of time defines a predictable process
exactly when $h$ is Borel measurable: the sets $C$ for which
$C\times\Omega\in\mathcal P$ form a sigma-algebra containing the intervals
$(s,u]$ and $\{0\}$, hence all Borel sets. Conversely, take any fixed
$\omega\in\Omega$ (a probability space is nonempty) and use the Borel
time-section property from 3(a) on every inverse image of an open set.
This single choice uses no choice axiom. In particular the
indicators $1_{[0,u]}$ and $1_{(0,u]}$ are predictable for every deterministic
$u\ge0$, and the process $s\mapsto 1_{s\le\tau(\omega)}$ for a stopping time
$\tau$ [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]] is predictable, since
$$\{(s,\omega):s>\tau(\omega)\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}(q,\infty)\times\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q\in\mathbb Q_{>0}}\bigcup_{n>q}(q,n]\times\{\tau<q\}$$
is a countable union of generators: for rational $q>0$ one has
$\{\tau<q\}=\bigcup_{q'<q,\ q'\in\mathbb Q}\{\tau\le q'\}\in\mathcal F_q$. The
complement of that set inside $[0,\infty)\times\Omega$ is the event of the
indicator, so $1_{[0,\tau]}$ is predictable; its left-continuity in the time
variable is the visual form of the same computation.

No completeness of the filtration and no right continuity of $(\mathcal F_t)$
is used or assumed. Apart from the inherited ambient assumption just recorded,
the constructions in this definition are choice-free.

Assume the Axiom of Choice [[def-axiom-of-choice]]. Fix a finite horizon
$T>0$, a probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ and a continuous-time
filtration $(\mathcal F_t)_{0\le t\le T}$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]]. A **simple
unit-jump counting process** is an adapted, càdlàg (right-continuous with left
limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued process $N$ with $N_0=0$,
$N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and $\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ for every
$0<t\le T$ outside one null event; here $\Delta N_t:=N_t-N_{t-}$.

An **at-risk process** is a predictable process
$Y:[0,T]\times\Omega\to\{0,1\}$, and an **intensity density** is a finite,
nonnegative predictable process $\lambda$. Form the Lebesgue integral
$$A_t:=\int_0^tY_s\lambda_s\,ds,\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
The **continuous intensity compensator contract** requires that this integral
be finite pathwise, that $A$ be continuous, adapted and predictable with
$A_0=0$, and that $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$. Set $M_t:=N_t-A_t$. The model
contract is the additional hypothesis that $M$ is a square-integrable
martingale relative to the stated filtration. Under this contract $A$ is a
continuous predictable compensator of $N$.

The displayed intensity density alone does **not** assert that $N-A$ is a
martingale, that such a process exists for a given $N$, or that the contract
follows from an empirical observation scheme. No general compensator-existence
theorem is included here. The Axiom of Choice is inherited from the
continuous-time martingale and conditional-expectation interfaces; no further
choice is used to state the model contract.

Assume AC, Countable Choice and Dependent Choice for the cited likelihood
and hazard-calculus interfaces. Fix $T>0$ and a common specified initial
history. Let $(P_\theta)$ be a supplied family of laws for actual simple,
non-explosive temporal point-process models on $(0,T]$ satisfying
[[def-temporal-point-process-and-conditional-intensity]], with jointly
measurable conditional history-update and waiting-time kernels. Let $P_0$
be the supplied unit-rate Poisson reference on the finite-pattern space
$$\mathsf X_T=\bigsqcup_{m\ge0}\Delta_m,\qquad \Delta_0=\{\varnothing\},\quad \Delta_m=\{(t_1,\ldots,t_m):0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T\},$$
equipped with the disjoint-union Borel sigma-algebra. For a pattern
$0<t_1<\cdots<t_m\le T$, let $h_{i-1}$ be the initial history updated by
$t_1,\ldots,t_{i-1}$. On each simplex, the laws are dominated by $P_0$ and
the following chosen density representative gives the Radon–Nikodym
derivative $P_0$-almost everywhere:
$$\frac{dP_\theta}{dP_0}(t_1,\ldots,t_m)=e^T\left(\prod_{i=1}^m\lambda_\theta^*(t_i\mid h_{i-1})\right)\exp\!\left(-\int_0^T\lambda_\theta^*(u\mid h_{u-})\,du\right).$$
Here $h_{u-}$ is the history immediately before $u$. Thus the likelihood as a
function of $\theta$ is proportional to the product of pre-event intensities
times the terminal integrated-hazard factor; $e^T$ is parameter-independent.
If an observed event has zero intensity, the density is zero; a finite
log-likelihood requires positive intensity at each observed event. For
$m=0$, the event product is the empty product $1$ and the terminal no-event
factor remains.

For marked patterns, let marks lie in a supplied measurable space with a
common mark probability measure $Q$. Here $h_i$ records all past event
times and marks, and the marked-history update is supplied and measurable.
Require that the supplied waiting-time kernels, conditioned on this full
marked history, satisfy the same temporal model; an unmarked marginal
waiting-time law alone is not this hypothesis. If each event also has a
supplied jointly measurable conditional mark density
$q_\theta(k_i\mid t_i,h_{i-1})$ relative to $Q$, and the reference uses
independent marks with law $Q$, evaluate the displayed intensity factors
on these marked histories and multiply the ratio by
$\prod_iq_\theta(k_i\mid t_i,h_{i-1})$. The ground intensity does not
determine a mark law.

For $x>0$, $\log$ is differentiable and
$$\log'(x)=\frac1x,\qquad \log x=\int_1^x\frac{dt}{t}.$$

Let $a, b \in \mathbb{R}$ with $a < b$ and let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be
continuous on $[a,b]$ ([[def-continuity-real]], [[def-interval]]) and
differentiable at every point of $(a,b)$ as a function on $[a,b]$
([[def-derivative]]). Then there is $c \in (a,b)$ with

$$f(b) - f(a) \;=\; f'(c)\,(b - a) .$$

Equivalently, since $b - a \ne 0$, there is $c \in (a,b)$ at which
$f'(c) = \bigl(f(b)-f(a)\bigr)/(b-a)$: the derivative somewhere inside equals
the average rate of change across the whole interval.

**Continuity on the closed interval cannot be dropped.** Differentiability at
every point of $(a,b)$ alone does not suffice: a function on $[0,1]$,
differentiable at every point of $(0,1)$ with derivative constantly $1$, for
which no $c$ works, is exhibited later on this page as a false statement, and
the companion page works the same witness out in full.
The exponential function is continuous and strictly increasing on $\mathbb R$.

The real exponential function is $C^\infty$, and for every $m\in\mathbb N$,
$$\exp^{(m)}=\exp.$$
In particular $(\exp)'=\exp$.

Let $a < b$ be reals, let $f : [a,b] \to \mathbb{R}$ be integrable
([[def-darboux-integral]]), let $F$ be its integral function
([[def-the-integral-function]]), and let $c \in [a,b]$ be a point at which $f$ is
continuous ([[def-continuity-real]]). Then $F$ is differentiable at $c$ as a
function on $[a,b]$ ([[def-derivative]]) and

$$F'(c) \;=\; f(c) .$$

At $c = a$ and $c = b$ this is the one-sided statement, which is what
[[def-derivative]] means at those points: every point of a nondegenerate interval
is a limit point of it, so $F'(c)$ is a meaningful symbol at every $c \in [a,b]$,
and the difference quotient is taken over $[a,b] \setminus \{c\}$.

**Consequently, if $f$ is continuous on the whole of $[a,b]$, then $F$ is a
primitive of $f$ there**: $F' = f$ at every point of $[a,b]$.

**Continuity at $c$ is a hypothesis and it cannot be dropped.** For an integrable
$f$ that is discontinuous at $c$, $F'(c)$ may fail to exist, and it may exist and
differ from $f(c)$; both are exhibited on the companion page, by
an integrable function with no primitive and by a false
statement about the integral function.

Assume the Axiom of Choice as in
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]. Fix a finite
horizon $T>0$, a probability space with an increasing filtration
$(\mathcal F_t)$ in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]], and an adapted
càdlàg (right-continuous with left limits), nondecreasing, integer-valued
process $N$ with $N_0=0$, $N_T<\infty$ almost surely, and jumps
$\Delta N_t\in\{0,1\}$ outside one null event. Such a process is **simple**:
its event times are strictly ordered,
$0<T_1<\cdots<T_{N_T}\le T$. It is **locally finite** when it has finitely
many events on every finite interval.

For conditional-law calculations, the model supplies a measurable history
space $(\mathsf H,\mathcal G)$, an adapted measurable history random element
$H_t$ recording the initial information and events observed through time $t$,
and a measurable update map $h\mapsto h\oplus u$ that appends an event at
time $u$. Write $\mathcal H_t:=\sigma(H_t)$ and let $H_{t-}$ record only
events strictly before $t$. Relevant exogenous covariates are included in
the supplied history. Measurability has the meaning of
[[def-measurable-function-between-measurable-spaces]]. Predictability is
measurability for the predictable sigma-algebra generated by
$(s,u]\times A$ with $A\in\mathcal F_s$ and the time-zero generators, as in
[[def-progressively-measurable-and-predictable-process]].

The model supplies a probability kernel $K_{t,h}$ on $(t,\infty]$ for the
next event time given history $h$ at time $t$
([[def-measure-kernel-and-probability-kernel]],
[[def-conditional-law-given-a-random-element]]); its finite-time density
versions are jointly measurable in $(t,h,u)$. The value $+\infty$ means that
no later event occurs. If the finite-time measure is absolutely continuous
with respect to Lebesgue measure
([[def-absolutely-continuous-with-respect-to-a-positive-measure]],
[[def-lebesgue-measure-and-the-lebesgue-sigma-algebra]],
[[thm-borel-sets-are-lebesgue-measurable]]), let $f_{t,h}$ be its supplied
nonnegative Radon--Nikodym density
([[def-radon-nikodym-derivative]]). Write
$S_{t,h}(u):=K_{t,h}((u,\infty])$ for its survivor and define its
**no-event conditional hazard** by
$$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u):=\frac{f_{t,h}(u)}{S_{t,h}(u)}\qquad\text{where }S_{t,h}(u)>0.$$
Assume these hazards are locally integrable on every finite interval. The
model also supplies a nonnegative predictable effective-intensity process
$\lambda^*$ compatible with these waiting-time hazards: for each history
$h$ at time $t$, on its supplied measurable no-event continuation up to
$u>t$, the pre-event intensity $\lambda^*(u\mid h_{u-})$ agrees with
$\lambda_{t,h}^*(u)$ for Lebesgue-almost every $u$. The jointly measurable
hazard representatives used in the event-density factors are these same
versions on their proper domains $u>t$. Compatibility with the predictable
process is a model requirement, not an evaluation of a waiting-time density
at its excluded left endpoint. This pre-event convention means the event
at $u$ does not change its own intensity.

The **temporal conditional-intensity model** requires both this
hazard-compatible conditional law and the separate counting-process
compensator contract of
[[def-counting-process-intensity-and-compensator-contract]]: if an at-risk
indicator $Y$ and intensity density $\lambda$ are separately specified, the
effective intensity is $\lambda^*=Y\lambda$; without an at-risk indicator,
it is $\lambda^*$. Then $A_t=\int_0^t\lambda^*(u)\,du$ is finite pathwise,
continuous, adapted and predictable, $\mathbb E[A_T]<\infty$, and $N-A$ is
a square-integrable martingale in the all-pairs convention of
[[def-continuous-time-adapted-process-and-martingale]]. At-risk exposure, if
present, is part of the effective intensity. The compensator clause is a
model assumption: a displayed hazard formula alone proves neither that a
process with this law exists nor that the martingale contract holds. No
stationarity or non-explosion claim follows from writing an intensity
specification.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of [[def-choice-function]]: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets ([[def-countable]]) has a choice function.

derivations.claim: For $\theta>0$, [F2] gives a simple finite-count Poisson process; for $\theta=0$, [F1] and the zero-rate count law make the process empty. Extend its count by $N_t=\eta((0,t\wedge T])$. For $0\le s<t$, $N_t-N_s$ is the count on $(s,t]\cap(0,T]$, independent of each finite cylinder of past Borel-set counts by [F1]. Indeed, refine any finite family of past Borel sets into the disjoint atoms of the finite Boolean algebra they generate. Each atom lies in $(0,s\wedge T]$ and is disjoint from $(s,t]\cap(0,T]$, so [F1] makes the atom-count vector independent of the future increment; the cylinder vector is a function of those atom counts. Such cylinders generate $\mathcal H_s$, so [F4] extends independence to the whole history sigma-algebra. Therefore $\mathbb E[N_t-N_s\mid\mathcal H_s]=\theta((t\wedge T)-(s\wedge T))$, and $N_t-A_t$ is a martingale for $A_t=\theta(t\wedge T)$. The effective intensity is $\lambda^*(t)=\theta\mathbf1_{(0,T]}(t)$, which is deterministic Borel and predictable by [F5]; its integral is $A_t$, continuous and bounded by $\theta T$. Also $N_t$ has finite second moment by [F3]. Thus $N-A$ is square-integrable and the Poisson process meets the compensator contract [F6].

Let $\mathsf H$ be the space of finite counting measures on $(0,\infty)$ with its evaluation sigma-algebra, and define $H_s(B):=\eta(B\cap(0,s\wedge T])$ for Borel $B\subseteq(0,\infty)$. Each $H_s$ is finite and measurable by the evaluation measurability of $\eta$, and $\sigma(H_s)=\mathcal H_s$. For finite $u>0$ put $h\oplus u=h+\delta_u$; the evaluation identity $(h\oplus u)(B)=h(B)+\mathbf1_B(u)$ shows that the update is jointly measurable and appends one event.

For a fixed finite pattern, its pre-event intensity at $t_i$ is $\mu+\alpha\sum_{j<i}e^{-\beta(t_i-t_j)}$. Integrating the baseline gives $\mu T$. For each event time $t_i$, the integral $\int_{t_i}^T e^{-\beta(u-t_i)}\,du$ equals $\frac{1-e^{-\beta(T-t_i)}}{\beta}$ by [F10], also when $t_i=T$, when both sides are zero. Summing these terms gives the displayed cumulative hazard.

For $s\ge0$ and $h\in\mathsf H$, supply the next-event kernel, supported on $(s,\infty]$, by $$K_{s,h}(C):=\int_{C\cap(s,T]}\theta e^{-\theta(u-s)}\,du+e^{-\theta(T-s)_+}\mathbf1_{\{\infty\in C\}}$$ for Borel $C\subseteq[0,\infty]$, where $x_+:=\max(x,0)$. Its finite-time mass is $1-e^{-\theta(T-s)_+}$, so each $K_{s,h}$ is a probability measure, including when $\theta=0$ or $s\ge T$. For fixed $C$, the finite-time term is $\theta e^{\theta s}\int_{C\cap(s,T]}e^{-\theta u}\,du$, a Borel function of $s$ because the tail integral is monotone on $[0,T]$ and zero for $s\ge T$; the atom mass is also Borel. The finite-time density $f_{s,h}(u)=\theta\mathbf1_{\{s<u\le T\}}e^{-\theta(u-s)}$ is jointly measurable in $(s,h,u)$. Independent increments give the same conditional survivor, $$S_{s,h}(u)=e^{-\theta((u\wedge T)-s)_+},\qquad u>s,$$ so the kernel is compatible with the observed finite-window Poisson law and supplies its terminal continuation after $T$. Its hazard is $\theta$ on $s<u\le T$ and $0$ for $u>T$, agreeing with $\lambda^*(u\mid h_{u-})=\theta\mathbf1_{(0,T]}(u)$ (and is identically zero at $\theta=0$). Thus the homogeneous survivor formula used in the likelihood is exactly $e^{-\theta(u-s)}$ for $s<u\le T$.

Substitute the Hawkes pre-event values and integrated hazard from step 1.3 into [F7]. This gives exactly the displayed Hawkes likelihood ratio. The calculation is conditional on a compatible process law and proves no existence, non-explosion, or stationarity property for the specification.

Within the observation window, $0\le s<u\le T$, the probability of no event in $(s,u]$ is $e^{-\theta(u-s)}$, so the no-event hazard is $\theta$ there. Applying [F7] to the $m$ events gives exact ratio $e^T\theta^m e^{-\theta T}$, including $m=0$ by the empty-product and terminal-survival conventions.

If $m>0$ and $\theta>0$, the log-likelihood is $\ell(\theta)=m\log\theta-\theta T$, with derivative $\ell'(\theta)=m/\theta-T$ by [F8]. It is positive for $0<\theta<m/T$ and negative for $\theta>m/T$. The mean value theorem [F9] therefore makes $\ell$ increase up to $m/T$ and decrease thereafter; at $\theta=0$ the likelihood is zero because $m>0$. Thus the unique maximum is $\widehat\theta=m/T$.

If $m=0$, the likelihood is $e^{-\theta T}$, which strictly decreases on $\theta\ge0$ because $T>0$ and the exponential is strictly increasing. Its maximum is attained at $\theta=0$. If zero were excluded from the parameter space, this case would have only a boundary supremum.
